name: Opening traps
goal: You can spot the common opening traps on f2 and f7 and in other openings, and avoid falling into them.
intro: An opening trap is a position where a natural-looking move loses at once. Most traps catch a player who grabs material, or develops a piece, without asking what the opponent can do next. In this Lesson you spring two famous traps and step around two others. The habit to take away: before each move, ask what your opponent's last move threatens, and what your own move leaves undefended.

parts.title: Legal's Mate: a pin that does not hold
parts.keyIdea: A piece pinned to the queen may still move when losing the queen leads to mate, or when the pinning piece is left undefended.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Philidor Defence. You are White. Black's bishop on g4 pins your f3 knight to your queen, and Black has just spent a move on ...h6 instead of developing. Is your knight really stuck?

notes.text: 5.Nxe5 takes a pawn and leaves your queen to be taken. If Black takes back with 5...dxe5, your queen now sees the bishop on g4, and 6.Qxg4 leaves you a pawn up. If Black grabs your queen, a mate follows.
Black took the queen with 5...Bxd1, the losing choice. 6.Bxf7+ leaves the king one legal move, to e7: the knight on e5 protects your bishop, and it also covers d7.

7.Nd5# is Legal's Mate. The d5 knight gives check and covers f6, the bishop on f7 covers e6 and e8, the e5 knight covers d7 and guards the bishop, and Black's own queen, pawn and bishop block d8, d6 and f8. Two knights and a bishop have beaten a whole extra queen.

parts.title: Legal's Mate in reverse, on f2
parts.keyIdea: Before you pin a piece to the queen, check whether your opponent could ignore the pin and mate you on f2.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Stafford Gambit. You are White and a pawn up, but Black's bishop on c5 already aims at f2, the weak square next to your king. In the game White pinned the f6 knight with 6.Bg5 and was mated three moves later. Find a safer developing move.

notes.text: 6.Be2 develops, gets you ready to castle and covers g4, a square Black's pieces want for an attack on f2. The tempting 6.Bg5, pinning the knight, would lose to Legal's Mate turned around: 6...Nxe4 7.Bxd8 Bxf2+ 8.Ke2 Bg4#, and other replies to 6...Nxe4 lose a lot of material.
Black's knight jumped to g4 anyway, aiming at f2 together with the bishop. 7.Bxg4 removes it. Black wins the piece back with 7...Qh4, which attacks your bishop and f2 at the same time.
8.g3 attacks the queen and blocks its path to f2. After 8...Qxg4 9.Qxg4 Bxg4 the queens come off, f2 is safe, and you are still a pawn up.

parts.title: The Elephant Trap
parts.keyIdea: A knight pinned to its queen may still move, if a check afterwards wins back more than the queen you give up.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Queen's Gambit Declined: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.cxd5 exd5. You are Black. White has just taken your pawn with 6.Nxd5, because your knight on f6 seems pinned to your queen by the bishop on g5. Is the pawn really free?
parts.line: Nxd5 Bxd8 Bb4+ Qd2 Bxd2+ Kxd2 Kxd8

notes.text: 6...Nxd5 takes the knight and leaves your queen to the bishop on g5. It looks like a blunder, but your bishop on f8 can now reach b4 with check, and White's only answer to that check will cost the queen.
White took your queen with 7.Bxd8. 7...Bb4+ checks along the diagonal to White's king, and the only way to block it is 8.Qd2.
8...Bxd2+ takes the queen with check, and White's king takes back.

9...Kxd8 takes the bishop. Count the captures: White took a pawn, your queen and a bishop; you took a knight, the queen and a bishop. You are a knight up for a pawn, all because White grabbed a pawn without asking what your answer could be.

parts.title: Mind the pin on the e-file
parts.keyIdea: When a pawn in front of your king is pinned, it cannot take a checking piece: keep a square free for the king.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess, in the Caro-Kann Defence. You are Black. White has just played the odd-looking 5.Qe2, putting the queen on the e-file with your king, and White's knight on e4 between them. In the game Black developed the most natural way and was mated on the next move. Find a safe developing move.

notes.text: 5...Ndf6 moves the d7 knight to f6, where it challenges the e4 knight, and d7 stays free for your king. The natural 5...Ngf6 would lose to 6.Nd6#, a smothered mate: the e7 pawn cannot take the knight because the queen on e2 pins it to your king, and your own pieces fill every square around the king. 5...Qc7, which covers d6, is also safe.
After 6.Nf3, 6...Nxe4 trades knights. White's queen has to take back, and it stands in the open where your pieces can attack it.
7...Nf6 develops with a threat to the queen on e4, so White must spend another move on it. You have side-stepped the trap and kept a sound position.
